targets.asr_text: Every later -life instinct I had woke up at once. Not memories, exactly. Shape, failure shape, conductive path, wet floor, metal, mana -bearing residue, people standing inside it. Back, Avenna moved immediately. Good. Arlo did not. He was staring at the pick. I grabbed the back of his coat and pulled. The purple line touched the trough. Copper rang. One clean note. Then the entire wet section of trough flashed violet along the seam.

A worker at the far vat turned toward us. Too close. Off the floor. He froze. Wrong response. I pointed at the dry platform beside him. Up. Now. That worked. He climbed. The line of light continued along the copper toward the raised reservoir. I knew what I would have done forty years later. Barrier under the seam. Cut the conductive path. Contain the spill. Buy everyone ten seconds. Simple. I put out my hand. Reached for mana. The pressure behind my eyes. A weak pulse down my arm. Then pain. No barrier. Not even close. For one ugly second I was fifty -nine again in my head and nineteen everywhere that mattered. The copper rang a second time. Reality did not care. Fine. No barrier. What did I have? People. Valves. Dry wood. Ash bins. Drain channel. A ceramic lid leaning against the wall.

Stupid. Instinct. Mana answered this time. Not a wall. Not even a proper barrier. A palm -wide shimmer snapped into existence in front of my hand. Thin. Crooked. Beautiful. The stream hit it. For less than a second, the liquid split around my palm instead of through it. Then the shimmer vanished. The rest struck the ceramic lid. I turned my face away. Hot droplets hit my sleeve. Not acid. Still unpleasant. Arlo stumbled back onto dry stone. The pipe stopped knocking. The violet line faded along the trough. Silence. Not complete silence. Dye house silence. Water dripping. Somebody breathing too loudly. A vat bubbling because nobody had told the other two vats that the scene was over. I looked at my hand. Nothing there. No barrier. Of course not. But it had been there. One breath less. Enough to change where the first part of the spray went. My arm started shaking. I lowered it before anyone could mistake that for drama. Avaina walked over.

Flow rate, higher for the same reason. How long before slowing? Longer than the first two full tests combined. Arlo's face changed. He was no longer defending the disk. He was collecting the failure. Good. Ivana knew her process. Arlo knew the material. I knew enough about later systems to recognize that neither of those jobs belonged to me. My job was somewhere else. Connections. What changed? What became dangerous? What mattered next? Heat. Flime under load. Concentration. Maybe manasalt. Maybe all of them. A month ago I would have tried to solve all five before leaving the building. Current me had recently been introduced to ceilings. I picked two. Arlo needed to reproduce the clog under warm continuous flow. Ivana needed a way to bypass the disk before pressure built if the flow slowed again. Everything else could wait until those answers existed. Arlo looked at me. That was almost approval. Ivana wanted the fitting checked first. Correct. Her shop, her order, we paid her. Mostly Arlo. I had just paid Val and was once again rich primarily in arguments.

and a bypass. He nodded. The dire had become part of the experiment, whether either of us liked it or not. Also good. I sat on the repaired stool and looked at my hand again. One pulse. One crooked shimmer. Enough to move liquid for less than a second. My sword had taken a month to become mine. Maybe mana would take longer. Maybe much longer. That hurt more than the sword had. Swordsmanship was something I had respected. Support was what I had become. There are failures that tell you what you cannot do. This one had done something worse. It reminded me what I wanted back. Outside, someone rolled a cart through the alley. The wheel hit a stone and rattled. Arlo started measuring clay. I had almost no money. Jorin left north soon. Our first customer wanted a refund, a repair, and possibly another filter. My old magic existed in my body as approximately one badly shaped breath. Progress. Apparently.

I counted twelve copper onto the counter. Cela counted them again, I had just counted them. She worked for the guild, different religion. She wrote my name into the ledger. Greg, bronze, ward support intake. I read it upside down. Ward support? You make planes. I make several things. This was technically true if failure counted as variety. She held out her hand. Show me.

I set the buckets down. Flue? Clay collar split last winter, the man said. We patched the plaster, should have pulled the whole section. He knew exactly where to put his hand on the wall without touching the hot part. I did not. Later construction codes ran clay liners all the way through walls like this. Later carol required clear stone around commercial stove flues. Later was currently useless. How far does it run? he pointed. Up there then left under the landing. The landing above us had six people on it. That seemed worth changing. I looked toward them. Everyone off the front stairs. Rear courtyard only. The man beside me snapped his fingers at the same time. You heard him. Move. People moved. I did not ask whether that made the order mine or his. The answer did not matter enough. He grabbed the iron poker from beside the stove and drove the point into the brown plaster. I caught his wrist. You open that, it gets air. It already has air. Not that much. And if we leave it, it eats the landing. He was right faster than I was. Annoying. I released him. Small opening first. That was the plan. Apparently I had improved it by repeating it. He punched through. The plaster broke inward. Orange appeared behind it.
